title: Lesson 5: Admitting Mistakes and Apologising Sincerely
summary: Mistakes happen. Dishonesty and blame-shifting create bigger problems. Admit what is yours, apologise sincerely, correct it and learn.

items.label: Duration
items.body: 45–60 minutes

items.label: Participants
items.body: All Zura Spa staff

items.label: Focus
items.body: Honesty, humility, accountability, sincere apologies, rebuilding trust and learning from mistakes

sections.title: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: Imagine a receptionist at Zura Spa receives a booking request for 4 p.m.
While entering the appointment, she mistakenly records it for 5 p.m.
The client arrives at 4 p.m., expecting her massage session to begin. Unfortunately, the assigned therapist is not ready because the appointment was recorded incorrectly.
The client becomes disappointed, and the supervisor begins investigating what happened. The receptionist realises that she made the mistake. She now has two choices.

Option A — Conceal the mistake: "The client probably gave the wrong time. I'm sure I entered what she told me." Later, the booking conversation confirms that the client requested 4 p.m. The mistake has now become a bigger problem because the receptionist was dishonest.

Option B — Admit the mistake: "I checked the booking conversation and realised I entered the wrong time. I'm sorry. I made the error, and I should have confirmed the appointment details before saving it. Let me help resolve the situation." The supervisor can now address the booking problem promptly.
Although the receptionist made a mistake, she demonstrated honesty and accountability.
The difference between these employees is not that one made a mistake and the other did not. The difference is how they responded after recognising the mistake.
At Zura Spa, every employee must understand that mistakes can happen, but dishonesty, deliberate concealment and blame-shifting can create more serious problems than the original error.
A professional employee should be willing to acknowledge genuine mistakes, apologise sincerely, correct what can be corrected and learn how to prevent similar problems.

sections.title: 2. What does it mean to admit a mistake?
paragraphs: Admitting a mistake means honestly acknowledging that an action, decision or failure to act was incorrect or did not meet the expected standard.
It involves recognising your responsibility rather than denying, concealing or transferring it to someone else.
Admitting a mistake does not mean accepting responsibility for everything that goes wrong. It means acknowledging the part that genuinely belongs to you.
Accountability begins with telling the truth about what happened.

sections.title: Examples at Zura Spa
list: A therapist: "I forgot to replenish the massage oil after my session."
A receptionist: "I entered the wrong appointment time."
A supervisor: "I communicated the schedule change too late."
A staff member: "I misunderstood the instruction and did not ask for clarification."

sections.title: 1. It builds trust
paragraphs: Colleagues and supervisors are more likely to trust employees who communicate honestly about errors.

sections.title: 2. It allows problems to be corrected quickly
paragraphs: When the actual cause of a problem is known, the team can focus on resolving it.

sections.title: 3. It protects teamwork
paragraphs: Taking responsibility prevents innocent colleagues from being blamed unfairly.

sections.title: 4. It supports healthy workplace relationships
paragraphs: Acknowledging wrongdoing demonstrates respect for people affected by our actions.

sections.title: 5. It creates learning opportunities
paragraphs: Understanding what went wrong helps employees improve procedures and habits.

sections.title: 6. It demonstrates professional maturity
paragraphs: Employees show that protecting their image is not more important than honesty and service quality.

sections.title: 4. The difference between a mistake, an excuse and dishonesty
paragraphs: These three concepts should not be confused.
A mistake may be accidental. An excuse may prevent improvement. Dishonesty can destroy trust. Accountability helps the team understand and resolve the problem.
Not every explanation is an excuse.
For example: "The clean towels had not arrived, so the room could not be fully prepared." This may be a legitimate explanation.
However, if the employee was also responsible for reporting the shortage and failed to do so, she should acknowledge that part of the situation.
Honesty requires presenting the full relevant facts, including your own responsibility.
table: Mistake
An error or incorrect action
Recording an appointment for the wrong time
Excuse
An attempt to avoid responsibility
"Everybody was busy, so it doesn't matter."
Dishonesty
Deliberately presenting false information or concealing relevant facts
Claiming the client gave the wrong time when the employee knows otherwise
Accountability
Acknowledging responsibility and addressing the outcome
"I entered the wrong time. I'll correct it and inform the supervisor."

sections.title: 5. Why employees sometimes find it difficult to admit mistakes
paragraphs: These concerns may help explain avoidance, but they do not justify dishonesty or deliberate concealment.
Management and supervisors also have a responsibility to encourage truthful reporting through fair and respectful treatment.

items.label: Fear of consequences
items.body: An employee may worry about receiving correction or disciplinary action.

items.label: Embarrassment
items.body: An employee may feel ashamed that others will discover an error.

items.label: Personal pride
items.body: Some employees believe admitting a mistake makes them appear weak or incompetent.

items.label: Fear of losing respect
items.body: An employee may worry that colleagues will no longer trust her abilities.

items.label: Desire to protect reputation
items.body: An employee may prefer to blame circumstances rather than acknowledge responsibility.

items.label: Previous negative experiences
items.body: If employees have previously been humiliated for admitting mistakes, they may become reluctant to report errors.

sections.title: 6. Understanding what a sincere apology means
paragraphs: A sincere apology is an honest acknowledgment that your action or omission caused harm, inconvenience or difficulty, accompanied by genuine responsibility and a willingness to make things right.
An apology should not be used merely to end an uncomfortable conversation.
It should demonstrate that the employee understands what happened and why it matters.

sections.title: Example — an unprepared treatment room
paragraphs: A therapist forgets to prepare a treatment room before the next appointment.
Weak apology: "Sorry, okay?"

Sincere apology: "I'm sorry I didn't prepare the room before the next appointment. I understand that this delayed the next therapist and affected the schedule. I'll complete the preparation now and make sure I check the room before leaving in future."
The second apology identifies the mistake, acknowledges its impact and includes a corrective action.

sections.title: 7. Five essential elements of a sincere apology

items.label: 1. Clearly acknowledge what happened
items.body: Identify the specific mistake instead of using vague language. "I entered the appointment time incorrectly."

items.label: 2. Express genuine regret
items.body: Communicate that you recognise the inconvenience or harm caused. "I'm sorry for the confusion this created."

items.label: 3. Accept your responsibility
items.body: Avoid immediately shifting blame. "I should have confirmed the details before saving the booking."

items.label: 4. Offer an appropriate corrective action
items.body: Explain what you can do to address the problem. "I'll update the booking and notify the relevant staff."

items.label: 5. Demonstrate improvement
items.body: Take practical steps to reduce the likelihood of repeating the mistake. "I'll verify appointment times against the client's confirmation before finalising bookings."

paragraphs: An apology becomes more meaningful when it is supported by changed behaviour.

sections.title: 8. Apologies that do not demonstrate genuine accountability
paragraphs: Some statements contain the word "sorry" but avoid responsibility.
A sincere apology focuses on responsibility and the impact of the behaviour.
An insincere apology may focus mainly on escaping blame or ending the conversation.
Employees should avoid apologising merely because they feel pressured.
Where responsibility is genuinely disputed, they can acknowledge another person's experience while clarifying the facts.
table: "Sorry if you were offended."
"I'm sorry I spoke disrespectfully to you."
"I'm sorry, but you made me angry."
"I'm sorry I raised my voice. I should have expressed my concern respectfully."
"Sorry, everybody makes mistakes."
"I'm sorry I made that mistake. I'll correct it."
"Sorry, but it wasn't really my fault."
"I'm sorry for the part I was responsible for. Let me explain the circumstances."
"Okay, sorry. Can we move on?"
"I understand what went wrong. Here's what I'll do to address it."
"I'm sorry you feel that way."
"I understand that my words were hurtful. I'm sorry I spoke that way."

items.label: O — Observe what happened
items.body: Identify the mistake accurately and understand the relevant facts.

items.label: W — Welcome responsibility
items.body: Acknowledge the part that genuinely belongs to you without unnecessary blame-shifting.

items.label: N — Name the impact
items.body: Recognise how the mistake affected colleagues, clients or operations.

items.label: I — Initiate correction
items.body: Take appropriate action or report the issue to someone authorised to resolve it.

items.label: T — Take steps to improve
items.body: Learn from the mistake and apply the lesson in future.

sections.title: OWN IT example
paragraphs: A therapist realises that she failed to communicate an important client preference during a handover.

She applies OWN IT. She identifies the omission, acknowledges her responsibility, informs the receiving therapist and supervisor as appropriate, apologises for the confusion and improves her handover process.
The goal is not simply to say "sorry." The goal is to ensure the relevant information reaches the right person and the mistake is less likely to happen again.

sections.title: 10. Admitting mistakes promptly instead of covering them up
paragraphs: One of the most important professional habits is reporting mistakes as soon as they are discovered.
Delaying disclosure can allow a small problem to become more serious.
Never conceal a mistake that could affect a client's safety, wellbeing or the accuracy of important workplace records.
Where immediate safety action is necessary, protect the client and obtain appropriate assistance before focusing on an apology.

sections.title: Example — an overlapping appointment
paragraphs: A receptionist notices that two clients have been assigned the same treatment room at overlapping times.
She may be tempted to remain silent and hope the issue resolves itself. However, waiting may cause unnecessary delays, confusion and client dissatisfaction.
Professional response: "I've noticed that two appointments overlap in Room 2. I made an error while updating the schedule. I'm sorry. Could we review the available options before the clients arrive?"

sections.title: Reporting becomes especially important when an error affects
list: Client safety or comfort.
Client consent or treatment preferences.
Appointment timing.
Confidential client information.
Payments or financial records.
Equipment or facility safety.
Hygiene and sanitation.
Another employee's ability to perform assigned duties.

sections.title: 11. Apologising to colleagues
paragraphs: Workplace relationships depend on mutual respect.
Employees may sometimes offend colleagues through careless words, missed responsibilities or misunderstandings.
An apology should address your behaviour, not become another opportunity to accuse the person you offended.

sections.title: Example — speaking harshly
paragraphs: A receptionist is overwhelmed by multiple client requests. A therapist asks a question, and the receptionist replies: "Can't you see I'm busy? Stop disturbing me!"
Later, the receptionist recognises that her response was disrespectful.

Sincere apology: "I'm sorry I spoke harshly to you earlier. I was overwhelmed, but that doesn't justify how I responded. I should have explained that I needed a moment. I'll communicate more respectfully next time."

The employee acknowledges her behaviour without denying the work pressure she experienced. She does not blame the colleague for asking a question. She identifies a better way to handle a similar situation.

sections.title: 12. Apologising to supervisors and management
paragraphs: Employees may sometimes fail to complete an instruction, misunderstand a responsibility or communicate inaccurate information.
When a genuine mistake occurs, employees should acknowledge it respectfully.
Supervisors should also be willing to acknowledge their own mistakes.
Accountability should apply across the workplace, not only to junior employees.

sections.title: Example — a forgotten maintenance report
paragraphs: A supervisor instructs an employee to report a maintenance issue. The employee forgets. The next day, the issue remains unresolved.

Professional response: "I'm sorry I didn't report the maintenance issue yesterday as instructed. I forgot to follow through. I'll report it now and ensure future issues are recorded and escalated promptly."

sections.title: What should be avoided
list: Pretending the instruction was never given.
Claiming the task was completed when it was not.
Blaming a colleague without evidence.
Creating a false explanation.
Becoming hostile when questioned.

sections.title: 13. Apologising to clients
paragraphs: Client-facing apologies require particular care because employees represent Zura Spa.
A sincere apology can help a client feel heard and respected.
However, employees must avoid promising remedies or compensation they are not authorised to provide.
An employee can apologise for an inconvenience without falsely admitting personal fault.
For example: "I'm sorry you experienced that delay. Let me investigate what happened." This acknowledges the client's experience while allowing the facts to be established.

items.label: Example A: Appointment delay
items.body: "I'm sorry your appointment has been delayed. I understand this is inconvenient. Let me confirm the updated timing and available options."

items.label: Example B: Failure to follow a preference
items.body: A client requests lighter massage pressure, but the therapist does not adjust promptly. "I'm sorry I didn't adjust the pressure when you requested it. Thank you for telling me. I'll reduce it immediately. Please let me know if you would prefer us to stop."

items.label: Example C: Incorrect information
items.body: A receptionist gives a client the wrong appointment time. "I'm sorry I provided the incorrect time. I've confirmed the correct details and will update you accordingly."

sections.title: 14. When an apology alone is not enough
paragraphs: Some mistakes require more than an apology.
An employee may sincerely regret an error, but the consequences still need attention.
The seriousness of a mistake determines the action required. Some errors need immediate escalation, documentation, corrective measures or formal review.

items.label: A payment-recording error
items.body: A receptionist records a client's payment incorrectly. Saying "I'm sorry" does not automatically correct the financial record. The employee must report the issue and ensure the appropriate authorised correction is made.

items.label: A hygiene-related mistake
items.body: A therapist notices that an item intended for clean use has been contaminated. An apology alone is insufficient. The item must be removed from use, the appropriate hygiene procedure followed and the issue reported where necessary.

items.label: A confidentiality breach
items.body: An employee accidentally shares client information with someone who should not receive it. The employee should promptly report the incident through the appropriate channel and follow instructions to contain the exposure. She should not attempt to conceal it or assume that deleting a message completely resolves the problem.

sections.title: 15. Rebuilding trust after a mistake
paragraphs: Admitting a mistake is the beginning of accountability.
Rebuilding trust often requires consistent behaviour over time.
Trust is strengthened when words and actions agree.
list: Tell the truth. Be accurate about what happened and what you know.
Acknowledge the impact. Recognise the inconvenience or harm caused.
Correct what you can. Take appropriate action within your responsibility and authority.
Follow through. Complete the actions you agreed to take.
Demonstrate improvement. Show through your work habits that you have learned from the experience.

sections.title: Example — a missed room-preparation checklist
paragraphs: An employee repeatedly forgets to update the room-preparation checklist.
After receiving correction, she apologises and promises to improve. However, she continues making the same omission without taking practical steps. Her apology may eventually lose credibility.
A more effective approach would be to identify why the checklist is being missed, adopt a reliable reminder or handover process and consistently complete the required checks.

sections.title: 16. Apologising without accepting false blame
paragraphs: Employees should not be pressured into apologising for misconduct or mistakes they did not commit.
If the employee later discovers that she contributed to the problem, she should acknowledge that contribution.
Employees should communicate accurately rather than making admissions they know are untrue.

sections.title: Example — a missed task with disputed responsibility
paragraphs: Two employees may disagree about who was responsible for a missed task.
One employee can acknowledge the inconvenience without falsely claiming responsibility.

Appropriate response: "I'm sorry the task was not completed and that it affected the schedule. My understanding is that I completed my assigned part. Could we review the responsibilities so we can establish what happened?"

sections.title: Important distinction

items.label: Apologising for an impact
items.body: "I'm sorry the client experienced a delay."

items.label: Admitting responsibility
items.body: "I'm sorry I caused the delay by entering the wrong time."

paragraphs: Both can be appropriate, but they mean different things.

sections.title: Case study A: The incorrect appointment
paragraphs: A receptionist enters a client's booking for the wrong time.
When the client arrives, the error becomes obvious. The receptionist initially considers blaming the client.
Expected lesson: Admitting errors promptly protects trust and makes it easier to resolve operational problems.
list: What mistake occurred?
Why might the receptionist want to conceal it?
What could happen if she blames the client?
How should she apologise?
What corrective action should follow?

sections.title: Case study B: The disrespectful response
paragraphs: A therapist is frustrated because a colleague has not completed a shared task.
She insults the colleague in front of other employees. Later, she realises that her response was inappropriate.
Expected lesson: Employees can apologise for disrespectful conduct while still addressing the original workplace concern.
list: Was the therapist's frustration understandable?
Did frustration justify the insult?
What should a sincere apology include?
How can she address the unfinished task separately?
What behaviour would demonstrate genuine improvement?

sections.title: Case study C: The unreported equipment issue
paragraphs: An employee notices a problem with equipment but forgets to report it.
Another employee later discovers the problem. The first employee is embarrassed and considers remaining silent.
Expected lesson: Honesty and timely escalation are essential when mistakes may affect safety or operations.
list: Why is prompt reporting important?
What could happen if the problem is concealed?
Who should be informed?
What should the employee acknowledge?
How can reporting procedures be improved?

sections.title: Case study D: The supervisor's mistake
paragraphs: A supervisor gives two employees conflicting instructions. The resulting confusion causes a delay.
The supervisor initially assumes the employees failed to cooperate. After reviewing the situation, she realises her instructions were unclear.
Expected lesson: Accountability and sincere apologies should apply to everyone, including supervisors and management.
list: Who should acknowledge the communication error?
How should the supervisor apologise?
Why is leadership accountability important?
What could prevent similar confusion?
How might the apology affect employee trust?

sections.title: 18. Practical group activity: Turn excuses into sincere apologies
paragraphs: Activity duration: 10 minutes.
Purpose: Help employees practise acknowledging mistakes, apologising sincerely and proposing appropriate corrective actions.
Divide participants into pairs or small groups. Each group should rewrite the statements below.
Expected outcome: Participants should understand that sincere apologies require honesty, responsibility and meaningful follow-through.
table: "It's not a big deal."
"I understand that my mistake affected the schedule. I'm sorry, and I'll help correct it."
"Sorry, but you annoyed me."
"I'm sorry I spoke disrespectfully. I should have communicated my frustration appropriately."
"Everybody forgets things."
"I forgot to complete the task. I'm sorry. I'll address it now."
"I thought someone else would do it."
"I misunderstood the responsibility. I should have clarified it earlier."
"Sorry if you felt bad."
"I'm sorry my words were hurtful. I should have spoken more respectfully."
"I already said sorry!"
"I understand that an apology alone may not resolve the issue. What can I do to help put things right?"

sections.title: Role-play
paragraphs: One participant plays an employee who made a genuine mistake. Another plays the colleague, client or supervisor affected.
The employee should practise the OWN IT method and include:
list: A clear acknowledgment of the mistake.
An appropriate apology.
Recognition of the impact.
A corrective action.
A practical improvement commitment.

sections.title: 19. Interactive assessment
paragraphs: Complete the Lesson 5 Knowledge Check at the bottom of this lesson. Choose an option, give your reason, then submit.
list: What does admitting a mistake mean? Accepting blame for every problem / Honestly acknowledging an error and the responsibility that genuinely belongs to you / Avoiding discussion until the problem disappears

Which statement is the most sincere apology? I'm sorry I entered the wrong appointment time. I'll correct it and verify bookings more carefully. / Sorry, but everybody makes mistakes. / Sorry if you were offended.

What should an employee do after discovering an error that may affect client safety? Keep quiet to avoid embarrassment / Wait to see whether anyone notices / Take necessary immediate safety action and promptly report the issue

Why is an apology alone sometimes insufficient? Because employees should never apologise / Because the mistake may also require correction, reporting or follow-through / Because apologies are always meaningless

What should you do if someone wrongly blames you for a mistake? Clarify the facts respectfully without falsely admitting responsibility / Accept the blame even when you know it is untrue / Insult the person making the accusation

sections.title: 20. Personal assignment
paragraphs: Each employee should answer the following questions in writing.
list: Explain what it means to admit a mistake in the workplace.
Identify five reasons employees may find it difficult to acknowledge mistakes.
Explain the difference between a mistake, an excuse, dishonesty and accountability.
Describe the five essential elements of a sincere apology.
Explain the OWN IT method in your own words.
Describe how you would apologise to a colleague after speaking disrespectfully.
Explain what you should do if you discover a booking error that may affect a client's appointment.
Describe why concealing a mistake can be more harmful than the original error.
Explain how employees can rebuild trust after making mistakes.
Describe how you would respond if you were wrongly blamed for an error.
Identify three habits you intend to develop to become more accountable at work.

sections.title: 21. Seven-day accountability challenge
table: Recognise and acknowledge your own mistakes without unnecessary excuses
Practise giving a clear, sincere apology when appropriate
Avoid blaming others for responsibilities that belong to you
Report errors promptly through the appropriate channel
Take practical action to correct a mistake or prevent its recurrence
Reflect on how honesty and accountability influence teamwork
Review your progress and identify one accountability habit to strengthen

sections.title: 22. Final lesson and takeaway
paragraphs: Every employee can make mistakes.
Mistakes do not automatically mean that an employee is dishonest, careless or incapable.
However, the way an employee responds after discovering a mistake reveals important aspects of their professional character.
At Zura Spa, employees should be willing to admit genuine mistakes, apologise sincerely, report important errors promptly and take appropriate corrective action.
They should avoid dishonesty, deliberate concealment, false accusations and blame-shifting.
Supervisors and management should also demonstrate accountability and create an environment where employees can report genuine errors without unnecessary humiliation.
Next topic: Giving and Receiving Constructive Feedback.

remember: Admitting a mistake does not make you weak; it demonstrates honesty and maturity. A sincere apology is not merely saying "sorry." It means recognising what went wrong, acknowledging your responsibility, considering how others were affected and taking meaningful steps to make things right. At Zura Spa, we build trust not by pretending to be perfect, but by being truthful, accountable and committed to continuous improvement.
